Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. The German-American architect and master of minimalism who distilled buildings to their essential elements, defining International Style modernism through glass-and-steel pavilions and open-plan spaces.

Mies van der Rohe lived from 1886 to 1969. He directed the Bauhaus school from 1930 to 1933 before fleeing Nazi Germany, later establishing American modernism at the Illinois Institute of Technology.

His Barcelona Pavilion, designed for the Spanish Exposition in 1929, was a floating glass and marble structure that redefined the concept of architectural transparency and spatial flow. He created the Farnsworth House in Illinois in 1951, a glass box elevated on steel supports demonstrating how a dwelling could dissolve boundaries between interior and exterior.

Mies pioneered the glass-and-steel curtain wall, enabling the design of the modern skyscraper and influencing buildings globally, including the Seagram Building in New York. He articulated the phrase less is more, emphasizing reduction to essential structural and aesthetic elements rather than ornament. He championed universal space—open floor plans without fixed walls, allowing flexible adaptation to inhabitants' needs.

His Chicago buildings, including Lake Shore Drive Apartments, became templates for postwar urban renewal, establishing the glass tower as an icon of modernism. He shared an industrial aesthetic with Le Corbusier, though Mies favored a more refined and austere minimalism. He co-directed the Bauhaus with Walter Gropius, and both shaped twentieth-century design education and modernism worldwide.

His approach stood in direct competition with Frank Lloyd Wright, who rejected Mies's machine-like purity as soulless and championed organic integration instead. The Bauhaus served as the institutional anchor of his career and his influence on postwar architecture globally.
